name: bonus_record_date_v1
author: claude-4.6-opus-agent-4
thesis: Stocks approaching a bonus issue or stock split record date exhibit a consistent pattern: buying pressure increases 2-5 days before the record date as retail investors buy to qualify for 'free' bonus shares (even though the economic value is unchanged post-adjustment). On the ex-date itself, the stock opens at the adjusted price but often overshoots to the downside as retail sellers who received bonus shares dump them. The intraday strategy: on the ex-date, buy the oversold bounce after the initial 30 minutes when selling pressure exhausts. The inefficiency is behavioral — retail investors treat bonus shares as 'free money,' creating predictable buying before and selling after the record date.
universe: NSE-listed stocks with bonus issue or stock split on ex-date
stock_filter: ADV(20) > ₹25 Cr; bonus ratio at least 1:2 or split ratio at least 1:2 (material); F&O listed preferred

indicators.name: Adjusted_Prev_Close
indicators.params: previous_close / (1 + bonus_ratio) for bonus; previous_close / split_ratio for split

indicators.name: Volume_Surge
indicators.params: sum(volume, bars 1-30) / (ADV(20) * 30/375) — ratio of first 30 min volume to expected

conditions: Open_Premium_Bps < -20 (stock opened below adjusted price — initial overselling)
Bar 30 has passed (initial selling pressure absorbed over 30 min)
Recovery_from_Low > 10 bps (price bouncing from session low)
Volume_Surge > 2.0 (high volume in first 30 min indicates selling exhaustion)
long.confirmation: close > VWAP_ExDate AND close > EMA(close, 10) (momentum turning positive after initial dump)

conditions: Open_Premium_Bps > 30 (stock opened well above adjusted price — retail euphoria)

exit.target: Close converges to Adjusted_Prev_Close (fair value): abs(Open_Premium_Bps) < 10 bps
exit.stop_loss: Price drops 30 bps below entry for longs / rises 30 bps above entry for shorts
exit.trailing_stop: After 20 bps profit, trail at 15 bps from high-water mark
exit.time_stop: 150 bars (2.5 hours) — ex-date adjustment should complete within first half of session
exit.signal_exit: VWAP_ExDate slope turns against position direction for 10 consecutive bars

risk.position_sizing: ₹75K per trade due to event-day uncertainty; reduce to ₹50K if VIX > 20

filters.time_filter: No entry before bar 30 (09:45 IST — let initial volatility settle); no entry after 14:00
filters.volume_filter: Volume_Surge > 1.5 (confirms active price discovery, not thin market)
filters.trend_filter: NIFTY 50 must be within ± 1% of previous close (neutral market day)
filters.spread_filter: Bid-ask spread < 10 bps (wider than normal on ex-date acceptable)
filters.event_filter: Must be bonus or split ex-date; not applicable to dividend ex-dates (different dynamics)
other_filters: Stock must have had normal trading (no halt, no circuit) on previous 3 sessions

edge.edge_decay_risk: Low — bonus/split ex-date dynamics are driven by retail behavioral biases (treating bonus as 'free money') that persist despite education; events are infrequent enough that systematic exploitation is rare

weaknesses: Bonus issues and stock splits are infrequent (10-20 material events per year among liquid stocks) — the strategy generates very few trades, unsuitable as a primary trading approach
The 'adjusted previous close' computation may differ from the exchange's official adjustment, causing the Open_Premium_Bps calculation to be slightly off — NSE adjusts using a specific methodology

Retail selling pressure on ex-date may be more persistent than the 30-minute window assumes — if the stock has a large retail holding (>30%), selling can continue for hours, and the 30-bar entry may be premature
prior_art: Grinblatt, Masulis & Titman (1984) on stock splits; Lamoureux & Poon (1987) on bonus issues; Indian market studies on ex-date effects in NSE working papers; behavioral finance literature on 'free shares' illusion
notes: Pre-screen upcoming bonus/split ex-dates from NSE corporate actions calendar. Compute the adjusted previous close the night before. The strategy works best for well-known, liquid names where retail participation is high (e.g., mid-cap IT, PSU banks with large retail investor bases).
